item.title: Clocks Fall Back November 1: Why America Still Can't Agree to Stop Changing Time
item.body:
In the early hours of **Sunday, November 1**, most of the United States will turn its clocks back one hour and return to standard time. Many people will enjoy an extra hour of sleep. Many will also be asking a familiar question: why are we still doing this?

Efforts to end the twice-a-year clock change have drawn support from both parties, from the White House and from large parts of the public. Legislation to make daylight saving time permanent has stalled in Congress again. Here is where the debate stands, what research says, and why states can't simply settle the matter themselves.

## How the current system works

The Uniform Time Act of 1966 created a national framework for daylight saving time (DST). Under today's rules, DST runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November.

States have limited choices under that law:

- **They can stay on standard time all year.** Hawaii and most of Arizona do this, along with several U.S. territories.
- **They cannot adopt permanent daylight saving time on their own.** That change requires an act of Congress.

Roughly twenty states have passed laws or resolutions that would adopt year-round daylight saving time if Congress permits it. Those measures sit idle until federal law changes.

## Why the push has stalled

The best-known proposal is the Sunshine Protection Act, which would lock in daylight time year-round. The Senate passed a version by unanimous consent in 2022, but it never received a vote in the House. Versions have been reintroduced in later sessions, and public statements of support from political leaders have followed. Still, no bill has reached the president's desk.

Several things keep the issue stuck:

1. **Disagreement over which time to make permanent.** Supporters of permanent daylight time want long summer-style evenings all year. Many sleep scientists argue permanent *standard* time is the better choice. Those two camps split the reform coalition.
2. **Regional differences.** Sunrise and sunset times vary widely across the country. Permanent daylight time would mean very late winter sunrises in some northern and western areas of a time zone.
3. **Limited floor time.** Congress has many competing priorities, and a change that touches every clock in the country is easy to postpone.

## What the sleep evidence says

Major sleep medicine organizations, including the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, have called for eliminating seasonal clock changes. Their preferred option is permanent standard time, because it more closely matches the body's natural light-dark cycle.

Researchers have linked the spring shift, when we lose an hour, to short-term disruptions such as less sleep and more daytime drowsiness. Some studies have also found small, temporary increases in heart attack and stroke risk in the days after the spring change. These findings describe averages across large populations, not a risk that every individual will experience, but they are a main reason health groups favor ending the switch.

## Safety and energy

The safety picture is mixed. Evening daylight can reduce some crimes and traffic collisions involving pedestrians at dusk. Darker winter mornings under permanent daylight time could raise risks for children walking to school and for early commuters. Research on crash rates after clock changes has also found short-lived spikes, especially after the spring change.

The original energy-saving argument is weaker than many assume. Modern studies generally find the effect on electricity use is small, and in some regions it is close to zero, because heating, cooling and electronics use have changed since the policy began.

## The economic argument

Business groups, retailers and the recreation and tourism sectors have often backed more evening daylight, arguing that people shop and spend more when it is light after work. Others point to costs from lost productivity after the spring change and from the confusion of coordinating schedules across time zones, especially in transportation, broadcasting and finance. Estimates of the economic effect vary a great deal depending on the method used, so they should be treated with caution.

## The lesson of the 1970s

The U.S. has tried this before. In 1974, Congress approved year-round daylight time as an energy-saving experiment. Public support dropped during the first dark winter mornings, and Congress repealed the measure the next year. That history is a major reason lawmakers and scientists urge care about which permanent time to choose.

## What to expect this November

For now, nothing changes in law. Sunrise and sunset will shift an hour earlier on November 1, and evenings will get dark sooner. Some practical steps can ease the adjustment:

- Shift bedtime 15 to 20 minutes earlier for a few nights beforehand.
- Get outdoor light in the morning after the change.
- Keep meal and wake-up times steady.
- Take extra care when driving at dusk, when drivers and pedestrians are adjusting to earlier darkness.

## The bottom line

Americans say in surveys that they want an end to clock changes, but they are less united on which time to keep. Until Congress picks one, and until states get the option or the mandate to act, the clocks will keep moving twice a year. Meanwhile, the evidence supports one clear conclusion: whichever time is chosen, staying on it all year is likely to be better than switching back and forth.

*This article is for general information and does not constitute medical advice. People with sleep or health concerns should speak with a qualified health professional.*
